name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Daniell cell at exact opposing voltage

questiontext.text: When an external opposite potential of exactly \(1.1\text{ V}\) is applied to a Daniell cell under standard conditions (\(1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\) concentration of \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions), what happens in the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Daniell cell under standard conditions generates an emf of \(1.1\text{ V}\). When an external opposing potential \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is applied, the net driving potential is \(1.1\text{ V} - E_{\text{ext}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
At \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), the external opposing potential exactly balances the cell emf, making the net potential difference zero.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Consequently, the chemical reaction stops altogether and no electrons or current flow through the cell.

answer.text: Electrons flow from copper to zinc and zinc is deposited.
No current flows and the cell reaction stops altogether.
Electrons flow from zinc to copper and copper is deposited.
The cell functions as an electrolytic cell with doubled current.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Condition for omitting a salt bridge

questiontext.text: Under which of the following conditions is a salt bridge NOT required in a galvanic cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A salt bridge internally connects the electrolytes of two separate half-cells to maintain electrical neutrality while preventing direct mixing of the two different solutions.

Step 2: Evaluation
When both electrodes dip into the same electrolyte solution, there is only a single common electrolyte compartment, so internal ionic conduction already occurs directly through that solution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, a salt bridge is not required when both electrodes dip in the same electrolyte solution.

answer.text: When both electrodes dip in the same electrolyte solution.
When the cell operates at \(298\text{ K}\) and \(1\text{ bar}\) pressure.
When the two half-cells contain different metal salt solutions.
When the cell emf is greater than \(1.1\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - IUPAC convention for galvanic cell representation

questiontext.text: According to the accepted IUPAC convention for representing a galvanic cell, which statement is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In standard galvanic cell notation, the oxidation half-cell (anode) is written on the left, the reduction half-cell (cathode) is written on the right, and a double vertical line represents the salt bridge.

Step 2: Evaluation
Under this convention, the cell emf is given by \(E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{right}} - E_{\text{left}}\), where both \(E_{\text{right}}\) and \(E_{\text{left}}\) are reduction potentials.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the anode is kept on the left, the cathode on the right, and \(E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{right}} - E_{\text{left}}\).

answer.text: The cathode is kept on the left and anode on the right, with \(E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{left}} - E_{\text{right}}\).
The anode is kept on the left and cathode on the right, with \(E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{left}} + E_{\text{right}}\).
The anode is kept on the left and cathode on the right, with \(E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{right}} - E_{\text{left}}\).
A double vertical line separates a metal electrode from its own electrolyte solution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Standard hydrogen electrode conditions and potential

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Individual half-cell potentials cannot be measured directly; therefore, the Standard Hydrogen Electrode is chosen as the reference half-cell.

Step 2: Evaluation
The SHE consists of a platinum electrode coated with platinum black dipped in a \(1\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq})\) solution with pure \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) bubbled at \(1\text{ bar}\) pressure, and it is assigned a potential of \(0.00\text{ V}\) at all temperatures.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, SHE has \(1\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\), \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at \(1\text{ bar}\), and zero potential at all temperatures.

answer.text: It uses \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at \(10\text{ bar}\) and has zero potential only at \(298\text{ K}\).
It uses a copper electrode in \(1\text{ M HCl}\) and has a potential of \(+0.34\text{ V}\).
It uses \(0.1\text{ M H}^{+}\) and has a potential of \(-0.76\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\).
It uses \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) at \(1\text{ bar}\) in \(1\text{ M H}^{+}\) and is assigned zero potential at all temperatures.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - Strongest oxidising and reducing agents in aqueous solution

questiontext.text: From the standard electrode potential series at \(298\text{ K}\) (\(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{F}_{2}/\mathrm{F}^{-}} = +2.87\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Li}^{+}/\mathrm{Li}} = -3.05\text{ V}\)), which pair correctly identifies the strongest oxidising agent and the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A higher positive standard reduction potential indicates a greater tendency for the oxidised species to gain electrons (stronger oxidising agent). A more negative standard reduction potential indicates a greater tendency for the reduced species to lose electrons (stronger reducing agent).

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{F}_{2}\) has the highest standard reduction potential (\(+2.87\text{ V}\)), making it the strongest oxidising agent. \(\mathrm{Li}^{+}/\mathrm{Li}\) has the lowest standard reduction potential (\(-3.05\text{ V}\)), making lithium metal (\(\mathrm{Li}\)) the strongest reducing agent.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{F}_{2}\) is the strongest oxidising agent and \(\mathrm{Li}\) is the strongest reducing agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Conversion between S cm-1 and S m-1

questiontext.text: Which of the following unit conversions for conductivity (\(\kappa\)) and resistivity (\(\rho\)) is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Unit conversion between \(\text{cm}\) and \(\text{m}\): \(1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}\) or \(1\text{ cm} = 10^{-2}\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
SI unit of conductivity is \(\mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}\) and SI unit of resistivity is \(\Omega\text{ m}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(1\text{ S cm}^{-1} = \frac{1\text{ S}}{1\text{ cm}} = \frac{1\text{ S}}{10^{-2}\text{ m}} = 100\text{ S m}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Similarly, \(1\text{ }\Omega\text{ m} = 100\text{ }\Omega\text{ cm}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, \(1\text{ S cm}^{-1} = 100\text{ S m}^{-1}\) is the correct relation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Effect of temperature on metallic conductance

questiontext.text: How does electronic (metallic) conductance behave when the temperature of a metal is increased?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrical conductance through metals is due to the movement of valence electrons through the metallic lattice.

Step 2: Evaluation
As temperature increases, thermal vibrations of metal kernels increase, obstructing electron flow. Hence, electronic conductance decreases with increase of temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Electronic conductance decreases with an increase in temperature, and the composition of the metallic conductor remains unchanged.

answer.text: It first decreases and then becomes infinite at \(298\text{ K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Effect of temperature on ionic conductance

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about electrolytic (ionic) conductance in aqueous solutions is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrolytic conductance is carried out by the movement of solvated ions in solution.

Step 2: Evaluation
With an increase in temperature, solvent viscosity decreases, ion mobility increases, and dissociation of weak electrolytes increases, so electrolytic conductance increases with temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, ionic conductance increases with an increase in temperature.

answer.text: It is independent of solvent viscosity and ion size.
It is caused solely by the movement of free electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Definition and dimension of cell constant

questiontext.text: The cell constant (\(G^{*}\)) of a conductivity cell is defined as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a conductivity cell with electrodes of cross-sectional area \(A\) separated by distance \(l\), resistance is \(R = \rho\frac{l}{A} = \frac{l}{\kappa A}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The geometric ratio \(\frac{l}{A}\) is called the cell constant \(G^{*}\). Rearranging gives \(G^{*} = R\kappa\), and its dimension is \(\text{length}^{-1}\) (e.g. \(\text{m}^{-1}\) or \(\text{cm}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(G^{*} = \frac{l}{A} = R\kappa\) with units of \(\text{m}^{-1}\) (or \(\text{cm}^{-1}\)).

answer.text: \(G^{*} = l \cdot A = R\rho\), having the dimension of \(\text{length}^{3}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Definition and value of one Faraday

questiontext.text: One Faraday (\(1\text{ F}\)) of electricity corresponds to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Charge on one electron \(e = 1.6021 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\); Avogadro's constant \(N_{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
One Faraday is defined as the magnitude of electric charge carried by one mole of electrons.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(1\text{ F} = N_{A} \times e\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(1\text{ F} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1} \times 1.6021 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C} = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1} \approx 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, \(1\text{ F}\) is the charge on one mole of electrons, equal to \(96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

answer.text: The charge on a single electron, equal to \(1.6021 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\)
The charge required to deposit \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions, equal to \(48243\text{ C}\)
The charge on one mole of electrons, equal to \(96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\)
A current of \(1\text{ ampere}\) flowing for \(1\text{ second}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Potential and constancy of a mercury cell

questiontext.text: Why does the cell potential of a mercury cell remain approximately constant at \(1.35\text{ V}\) throughout its lifetime?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the Nernst equation, cell potential changes over time if the concentrations of dissolved ions participating in the overall cell reaction vary during discharge.

Step 2: Evaluation
The overall reaction of a mercury cell is \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\). It involves only pure solids and liquids, with no ions in solution whose concentration can change.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the cell potential remains constant at approximately \(1.35\text{ V}\) throughout its life.

answer.text: Because it is a secondary cell that recharges continuously from air.
Because the overall reaction involves no ions in solution whose concentration can change.
Because the \(\mathrm{KOH}\) electrolyte concentration doubles during discharge.
Because ammonia forms a stable complex with mercury ions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12 - Efficiency of fuel cells versus thermal plants

questiontext.text: What is the approximate electrical energy conversion efficiency of a \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\text{–}\mathrm{O}_{2}\) fuel cell compared to a conventional thermal power plant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thermal plants convert chemical energy into heat, then steam, then mechanical energy, and finally electricity, incurring significant thermodynamic losses. Fuel cells convert the Gibbs energy of fuel combustion directly into electrical energy.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fuel cells achieve an efficiency of about \(70\%\), whereas thermal power plants have an efficiency of about \(40\%\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, fuel cells operate at about \(70\%\) efficiency compared to \(40\%\) for thermal plants.

answer.text: About \(40\%\) for fuel cells compared to \(70\%\) for thermal plants
About \(25\%\) for fuel cells compared to \(50\%\) for thermal plants
About \(95\%\) for fuel cells compared to \(10\%\) for thermal plants
About \(70\%\) for fuel cells compared to \(40\%\) for thermal plants

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Standard emf of Daniell cell calculation

questiontext.text: Given \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\) and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\), what is the standard emf of the Daniell cell \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq, 1 M}) \parallel \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq, 1 M}) \mid \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\) (right/cathode), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\) (left/anode).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard reduction potentials are used directly in \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{right}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{left}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} - E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.34\text{ V} - (-0.76\text{ V}) = 0.34\text{ V} + 0.76\text{ V} = 1.10\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The positive emf confirms the spontaneous reaction \(\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + \mathrm{Cu}\). The standard emf is \(1.10\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Copper silver galvanic cell representation and emf

questiontext.text: For the spontaneous cell reaction \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), given \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\) and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\), what is the correct cell representation and standard emf?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\); \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Copper is oxidised (anode, placed on the left) and silver ions are reduced (cathode, placed on the right).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{right}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{left}} = E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} - E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Cell representation: \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} \mid \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \parallel \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\).
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.80\text{ V} - 0.34\text{ V} = 0.46\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Positive \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) confirms spontaneity as written. Thus, the representation is \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} \mid \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \parallel \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\) and \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.46\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Behaviour of copper in hydrochloric and nitric acids

questiontext.text: Copper does not dissolve in hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) to liberate \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\), whereas it dissolves in nitric acid (\(\mathrm{HNO}_{3}\)). Which explanation is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a metal to dissolve in an acid via \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) evolution, \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions must oxidise the metal, which requires \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{metal}} < E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_{2}}\) (\(0.00\text{ V}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Since \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V} > 0.00\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions cannot oxidise \(\mathrm{Cu}\), so \(\mathrm{Cu}\) does not dissolve in \(\mathrm{HCl}\). In \(\mathrm{HNO}_{3}\), nitrate ions (\(\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}\), \(E^{\ominus} = +0.97\text{ V}\)) act as the oxidising agent and oxidise \(\mathrm{Cu}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{Cu}\) does not dissolve in \(\mathrm{HCl}\) because \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) cannot oxidise \(\mathrm{Cu}\), whereas in \(\mathrm{HNO}_{3}\) it is oxidised by \(\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}\) ions.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions cannot oxidise \(\mathrm{Cu}\), whereas in nitric acid \(\mathrm{Cu}\) is oxidised by \(\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}\) ions.
\(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) ions reduce \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) back to \(\mathrm{Cu}\), while \(\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}\) precipitates \(\mathrm{Cu}\).
\(\mathrm{Cu}\) has a negative standard reduction potential, so it only reacts with oxidising acids.
\(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) gas oxidises \(\mathrm{Cu}\) in \(\mathrm{HNO}_{3}\) but not in \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q16 - Storing copper sulphate solution in a zinc pot

questiontext.text: Can an aqueous solution of copper sulphate (\(\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}\)) be safely stored in a zinc pot? (Given \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\) and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A metal with a lower standard reduction potential displaces a metal with a higher standard reduction potential from its salt solution.

Step 2: Evaluation
Since \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V} < E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\), zinc is a stronger reducing agent than copper and reacts spontaneously with \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions: \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\) (\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +1.10\text{ V}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}\) solution cannot be stored in a zinc pot because zinc will dissolve and displace copper.

answer.text: Yes, because \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) cannot oxidise \(\mathrm{Zn}\) under standard conditions.
No, because \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is more reactive and displaces \(\mathrm{Cu}\) from \(\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}\) solution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q17 - Feasibility of redox reactions using standard potentials

questiontext.text: Using the standard reduction potentials: \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{I}_{2}/\mathrm{I}^{-}} = +0.54\text{ V}\), and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Br}_{2}/\mathrm{Br}^{-}} = +1.09\text{ V}\), which of the following reactions is NOT feasible under standard conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A redox reaction is feasible if \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{anode}} > 0\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Reaction
- \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) oxidising \(\mathrm{I}^{-}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23\text{ V} > 0\) (feasible).
- \(\mathrm{Br}_{2}\) oxidising \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.09 - 0.77 = +0.32\text{ V} > 0\) (feasible).
- \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\) oxidising \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.80 - 0.77 = +0.03\text{ V} > 0\) (feasible).
- \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) oxidising \(\mathrm{Br}^{-}\): \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.77 - 1.09 = -0.32\text{ V} < 0\) (not feasible).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the reaction between \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})\) and \(\mathrm{Br}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\) is not feasible.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q18 - Concentration dependence of Daniell cell potential

questiontext.text: For a Daniell cell, \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\), how does the cell potential \(E_{\text{cell}}\) change when \([\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]\) is increased and \([\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]\) is decreased?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the Nernst equation for the Daniell cell at \(298\text{ K}\): \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2}\log\frac{[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Increasing \([\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]\) and decreasing \([\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]\) decreases the ratio \(\frac{[\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}\), making the subtracted logarithmic term smaller (or negative).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(E_{\text{cell}}\) increases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q19 - Nernst equation for nickel silver cell

questiontext.text: Which expression correctly represents the Nernst equation for the cell \(\mathrm{Ni(s)} \mid \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \parallel \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The balanced cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Ni(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), transferring \(n = 2\text{ mol}\) of electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pure solids have unit activity, so the reaction quotient is \(Q = \frac{[\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}]^{2}}\). Substituting into \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q\) gives \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{2F}\ln\frac{[\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}]^{2}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct Nernst equation is \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{2F}\ln\frac{[\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}]^{2}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q20 - Equilibrium constant of Daniell cell at 298 K

questiontext.text: For the Daniell cell at \(298\text{ K}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\). What is the approximate value of the equilibrium constant \(K_{c}\) for the reaction \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), \(T = 298\text{ K}\), \(n = 2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At equilibrium, \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\) and \(Q = K_{c}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n}\log K_{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\log K_{c} = \frac{1.1 \times 2}{0.059} = \frac{2.2}{0.059} = 37.288\]
Taking antilog: \(K_{c} = 10^{37.288} \approx 2 \times 10^{37}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A large positive \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) yields a very large \(K_{c}\), confirming the reaction proceeds nearly to completion. Thus, \(K_{c} \approx 2 \times 10^{37}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q21 - Equilibrium constant of copper silver reaction

questiontext.text: Calculate the equilibrium constant \(K_{c}\) at \(298\text{ K}\) for the reaction \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), given \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.46\text{ V}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.46\text{ V}\), \(T = 298\text{ K}\), \(n = 2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At equilibrium, \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n}\log K_{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\log K_{c} = \frac{0.46 \times 2}{0.059} = \frac{0.92}{0.059} = 15.59 \approx 15.6\]
\[K_{c} = 10^{15.59} = 3.92 \times 10^{15}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The exponent \(15.6\) places \(K_{c}\) between \(10^{15}\) and \(10^{16}\). Thus, \(K_{c} = 3.92 \times 10^{15}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q22 - Standard Gibbs energy change for Daniell cell

questiontext.text: The standard electrode potential for the Daniell cell is \(1.1\text{ V}\). Calculate the standard Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus}\)) for the reaction \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\) (take \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), \(n = 2\), \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Reversible electrical work done by the galvanic cell equals the decrease in Gibbs energy.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -2 \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1} \times 1.1\text{ V} = -212271.4\text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx -212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The negative sign confirms spontaneity. Therefore, \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q23 - Effect of doubling stoichiometry on Gibbs energy and emf

questiontext.text: If the cell reaction \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\) is written as \(2\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Cu(s)}\), how do \(\Delta_{r}G\) and \(E_{\text{cell}}\) change?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cell potential \(E_{\text{cell}}\) is an intensive parameter, whereas Gibbs energy change \(\Delta_{r}G = -nFE_{\text{cell}}\) is an extensive thermodynamic property.

Step 2: Evaluation
Doubling the stoichiometric coefficients doubles the number of moles of electrons transferred from \(n = 2\) to \(n = 4\). Consequently, \(\Delta_{r}G\) changes from \(-2FE_{\text{cell}}\) to \(-4FE_{\text{cell}}\) (doubles), while \(E_{\text{cell}}\) remains unchanged.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\Delta_{r}G\) doubles while \(E_{\text{cell}}\) remains unchanged.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q24 - Definition and temperature range of superconductors

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly describes superconductors?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Superconductors are materials that exhibit zero electrical resistivity (and hence infinite conductivity) below a critical temperature.

Step 2: Evaluation
Earlier only metals and their alloys at \(0\text{ to }15\text{ K}\) were known to be superconductors, but several ceramic materials and mixed oxides also show superconductivity at temperatures as high as \(150\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, superconductors have zero resistivity or infinite conductivity, and certain ceramics/mixed oxides exhibit this up to \(150\text{ K}\).

answer.text: They have infinite resistivity and zero conductivity at room temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q25 - Organic conducting polymers

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of an electronically conducting organic polymer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain conjugated organic polymers such as polyacetylene (when exposed to iodine vapours), polyaniline, polypyrrole, and polythiophene exhibit metallic lustre and electronic conductivity.

Step 2: Evaluation
Among the choices, polyaniline is a well-known electronically conducting organic polymer, whereas teflon and glass are insulators and pure water is a weak ionic conductor.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, polyaniline is an electronically conducting organic polymer.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q26 - Unit conversion for molar conductivity

questiontext.text: How are the SI unit (\(\mathrm{S\ m^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)) and the commonly used CGS unit (\(\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)) of molar conductivity related?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm} = 10^{2}\text{ cm}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Molar conductivity units involve \(\text{length}^{2}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(1\text{ m}^{2} = (10^{2}\text{ cm})^{2} = 10^{4}\text{ cm}^{2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Therefore, \(1\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^{4}\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), or equivalently \(1\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, \(1\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^{4}\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q27 - Molar conductivity of 0.20 M KCl solution

questiontext.text: The conductivity of a \(0.20\text{ M}\) solution of \(\mathrm{KCl}\) at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(0.0248\text{ S cm}^{-1}\). What is its molar conductivity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molarity \(c = 0.20\text{ mol L}^{-1}\), conductivity \(\kappa = 0.0248\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Use the CGS-molarity conversion factor \(1000\text{ cm}^{3}\text{ L}^{-1}\) so that \(\Lambda_{m}\) is obtained in \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Lambda_{m} = \frac{0.0248\text{ S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\text{ cm}^{3}\text{ L}^{-1}}{0.20\text{ mol L}^{-1}} = \frac{24.8}{0.20} = 124\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units: \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\). The molar conductivity is \(124\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q28 - Cell constant from 0.001 M KCl measurement

questiontext.text: The resistance of a conductivity cell containing \(0.001\text{ M KCl}\) solution at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(1500\text{ }\Omega\). If the conductivity of \(0.001\text{ M KCl}\) solution at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\), what is the cell constant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Resistance \(R = 1500\text{ }\Omega\), conductivity \(\kappa = 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Cell constant \(G^{*}\) has units of \(\text{cm}^{-1}\) when \(\kappa\) is in \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[G^{*} = R \times \kappa\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[G^{*} = 1500\text{ }\Omega \times 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1} = 1.5 \times 0.146\text{ cm}^{-1} = 0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\Omega \cdot \mathrm{S} = 1\), the unit reduces to \(\text{cm}^{-1}\). The cell constant is \(0.219\text{ cm}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q29 - Opposite trends of conductivity and molar conductivity on dilution

questiontext.text: Why does molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_{m}\)) increase with dilution even though conductivity (\(\kappa\)) decreases with dilution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conductivity \(\kappa\) is the conductance of one unit volume of solution, whereas molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{m} = \kappa V\) is the conductance of the volume \(V\) of solution containing one mole of electrolyte.

Step 2: Evaluation
On dilution, the number of ions per unit volume decreases, causing \(\kappa\) to decrease. However, the volume \(V\) containing one mole of electrolyte increases, and this increase in \(V\) more than compensates for the decrease in \(\kappa\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\Lambda_{m} = \kappa V\) increases upon dilution.

answer.text: Because the cell constant \(G^{*}\) increases with dilution.
Because the number of ions per unit volume increases on dilution.
Because the increase in volume \(V\) containing \(1\text{ mol}\) of electrolyte more than compensates for the decrease in \(\kappa\).
Because interionic attractions increase on dilution, speeding up ion motion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q30 - Limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid

questiontext.text: If \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) values for \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), \(\mathrm{HCl}\), and \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COONa}\) are \(126.4\), \(425.9\), and \(91.0\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) respectively at \(298\text{ K}\), what is \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) for acetic acid (\(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl}) = 126.4\), \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) = 425.9\), \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaAc}) = 91.0\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
By Kohlrausch law, limiting molar conductivity is additive over individual ionic contributions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HAc}) = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) + \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaAc}) - \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl})\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HAc}) = (425.9 + 91.0 - 126.4)\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 516.9 - 126.4 = 390.5\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) contributions cancel out cleanly. Thus, \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}) = 390.5\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q31 - Determining limiting molar conductivity of water

questiontext.text: Using Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions, how can the limiting molar conductivity of water, \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})\), be determined from strong electrolytes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At infinite dilution, \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{OH}^{-}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Combining strong electrolytes: \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) + \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaOH}) - \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl}) = (\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl}^{-}}) + (\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Na}^{+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{OH}^{-}}) - (\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Na}^{+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl}^{-}}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{OH}^{-}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}) = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) + \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaOH}) - \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q32 - Faraday second law of electrolysis

questiontext.text: According to Faraday's second law of electrolysis, when the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytic solutions, the amounts of different substances liberated are proportional to their:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
One mole of electrons (\(1\text{ F}\)) deposits or liberates one gram-equivalent of any substance, where chemical equivalent weight equals atomic mass divided by the number of electrons required to reduce the ion.

Step 2: Evaluation
Therefore, for a fixed quantity of electricity \(Q\), the masses of different substances liberated are directly proportional to their chemical equivalent weights.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the amounts liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q33 - Charge required to reduce 1 mol of dichromate ions

questiontext.text: Consider the reduction reaction: \(\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 14\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 6\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 7\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\). What quantity of electricity in coulombs is needed to reduce \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}\) (take \(1\text{ F} = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Moles of \(\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-} = 1\text{ mol}\), \(n = 6\text{ mol}\) of electrons per mole of \(\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}\), \(1\text{ F} = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume \(100\%\) current efficiency.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[Q = n \times F\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[Q = 6\text{ mol} \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1} = 578922\text{ C}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each \(\mathrm{Cr}\) atom changes oxidation state from \(+6\) to \(+3\), so \(2\text{ Cr}\) atoms require \(6\) electrons. Thus, \(578922\text{ C}\) is required.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q34 - Products of electrolysis of aqueous NaCl

questiontext.text: During the electrolysis of an aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) using inert platinum electrodes, what are the overall products formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In aqueous \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), both \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}/\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) ions and water compete at the electrodes.

Step 2: Evaluation
At the cathode, reduction of water/protons (\(E^{\ominus} = 0.00\text{ V}\)) is preferred over \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) (\(E^{\ominus} = -2.71\text{ V}\)), producing \(\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\). At the anode, \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\) in preference to \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) due to the overpotential of oxygen. \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\) remain in solution as \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the products are \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q35 - Anodic product in concentrated sulphuric acid electrolysis

questiontext.text: During the electrolysis of sulphuric acid using platinum electrodes, which anodic product is preferred at higher concentrations of \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At the anode during \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\) electrolysis, two oxidation processes compete: oxidation of water to \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) (\(E^{\ominus} = +1.23\text{ V}\)) and oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}\) to \(\mathrm{S}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{8}^{2-}\) (\(E^{\ominus} = +1.96\text{ V}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
For dilute \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\), water oxidation to \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) is preferred. However, at higher concentrations of \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\), the concentration effect shifts the electrode potential and favours the oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}\) to peroxodisulphate ions, \(\mathrm{S}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{8}^{2-}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{S}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{8}^{2-}(\mathrm{aq})\) is preferred at higher concentrations of \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q36 - Electrolytic refining of impure copper

questiontext.text: In the industrial electrolytic refining of copper using an aqueous \(\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}\) bath, how are the electrodes arranged?

generalfeedback.text:

In an electrolytic cell, oxidation (dissolution) occurs at the anode and reduction (deposition) occurs at the cathode.

Impure copper is made the anode so that it dissolves as \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions on passing current, and pure copper is deposited on the cathode (\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, impure copper is made the anode and pure copper is deposited at the cathode.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q38 - Recharging chemistry of lead storage battery

questiontext.text: When a lead storage battery is recharged by passing current in the opposite direction, what happens to the \(\mathrm{PbSO}_{4}(\mathrm{s})\) present on the electrodes?

generalfeedback.text:

During discharge of a lead storage battery, both the lead anode and the \(\mathrm{PbO}_{2}\) cathode are converted into \(\mathrm{PbSO}_{4}(\mathrm{s})\), consuming \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{PbSO}_{4}(\mathrm{s})\) is converted into \(\mathrm{Pb}\) and \(\mathrm{PbO}_{2}\) on the respective electrodes, regenerating \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q39 - Nickel cadmium cell discharge reaction

questiontext.text: Which equation represents the overall discharge reaction of a rechargeable nickel–cadmium cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A nickel–cadmium cell is a secondary battery with a longer life than a lead storage cell, using cadmium and nickel(III) hydroxide in an alkaline medium.

During discharge, cadmium is oxidised to \(\mathrm{CdO(s)}\) while \(\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{3}(\mathrm{s})\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{2}(\mathrm{s})\): \(\mathrm{Cd(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{3}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CdO(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{2}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the overall discharge reaction is \(\mathrm{Cd(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{3}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CdO(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ni(OH)}_{2}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O(l)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q44 - Cell potential of magnesium silver nonstandard cell

questiontext.text: Calculate the emf at \(298\text{ K}\) of the cell \(\mathrm{Mg(s)} \mid \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(0.130\text{ M}) \parallel \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(0.0001\text{ M}) \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\), given \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\), \([\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}] = 0.130\text{ M}\), \([\mathrm{Ag}^{+}] = 0.0001\text{ M} = 10^{-4}\text{ M}\), \(T = 298\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Cell reaction: \(\mathrm{Mg(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), with \(n = 2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2}\log\frac{[\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}]^{2}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\frac{[\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}]^{2}} = \frac{0.130}{(10^{-4})^{2}} = 0.130 \times 10^{8} = 1.30 \times 10^{7}\]
\[\log(1.30 \times 10^{7}) = 7 + \log(1.30) = 7 + 0.1139 = 7.1139\]
\[E_{\text{cell}} = 3.17 - \frac{0.059}{2}(7.1139) = 3.17 - 0.21 = 2.96\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because \([\mathrm{Ag}^{+}]\) is very small, \(E_{\text{cell}} < E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\). Thus, \(E_{\text{cell}} = 2.96\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q45 - Emf of nickel silver nonstandard cell

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q46 - Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant of ferric iodide cell

questiontext.text: The cell in which the reaction \(2\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{I}^{-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{I}_{2}(\mathrm{s})\) occurs has \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\). generalfeedback.text:

\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\text{ V}\), \(T = 298\text{ K}\), \(n = 2\), \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard conditions apply to all reactants and products.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -nFE^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Negative \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus}\) and \(K_{c} \gg 1\) are consistent. Thus, \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -45.54\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(K_{c} = 9.62 \times 10^{7}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q47 - Standard cell potential and Gibbs energy of Cr-Cd cell

questiontext.text: For the galvanic cell reaction \(2\mathrm{Cr(s)} + 3\mathrm{Cd}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 3\mathrm{Cd(s)}\), given \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr}} = -0.74\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cd}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cd}} = -0.40\text{ V}\), and \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\), calculate \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\) and \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q48 - Standard emf and Gibbs energy of watch button cell

Both \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} > 0\) and \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} < 0\) confirm spontaneous operation. Thus, \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\text{ V}\) and \(\Delta_{r}G^{\ominus} = -212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q49 - Nernst emf of magnesium copper nonstandard cell

questiontext.text: Calculate the emf at \(298\text{ K}\) of the cell \(\mathrm{Mg(s)} \mid \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(0.001\text{ M}) \parallel \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(0.0001\text{ M}) \mid \mathrm{Cu(s)}\), given \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}} = -2.36\text{ V}\) and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\).

generalfeedback.text:

\(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}} = -2.36\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\), \([\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}] = 10^{-3}\text{ M}\), \([\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}] = 10^{-4}\text{ M}\), \(n = 2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Cell reaction: \(\mathrm{Mg(s)} + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} - E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \([\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}] > [\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]\), \(E_{\text{cell}}\) is slightly less than \(2.70\text{ V}\). Thus, \(E_{\text{cell}} = 2.67\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q50 - Nernst emf of iron hydrogen cell

questiontext.text: Calculate the emf at \(298\text{ K}\) of the cell \(\mathrm{Fe(s)} \mid \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(0.001\text{ M}) \parallel \mathrm{H}^{+}(1\text{ M}) \mid \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g, 1 bar}) \mid \mathrm{Pt(s)}\), given \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}/\mathrm{Fe}} = -0.44\text{ V}\).

Low \([\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]\) favours the forward reaction, raising \(E_{\text{cell}}\) above \(0.44\text{ V}\). Thus, \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0.53\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q51 - Nernst emf of tin hydrogen nonstandard cell

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q53 - Conductivity and molar conductivity of 0.02 M KCl

questiontext.text: The resistance of a conductivity cell filled with \(0.1\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution is \(100\text{ }\Omega\) (conductivity \(= 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\)). When filled with \(0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution, its resistance is \(520\text{ }\Omega\). What are the conductivity and molar conductivity of the \(0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(R_{1} = 100\text{ }\Omega\), \(\kappa_{1} = 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\); \(R_{2} = 520\text{ }\Omega\), \(c_{2} = 0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1} = 20\text{ mol m}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The cell constant \(G^{*}\) is fixed for the same conductivity cell.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[G^{*} = R_{1}\kappa_{1}, \quad \kappa_{2} = \frac{G^{*}}{R_{2}}, \quad \Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa_{2}}{c_{2}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[G^{*} = 100\text{ }\Omega \times 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1} = 129\text{ m}^{-1}\]
\[\kappa_{2} = \frac{129\text{ m}^{-1}}{520\text{ }\Omega} = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\]
\[\Lambda_{m} = \frac{0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}}{20\text{ mol m}^{-3}} = 0.0124\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
As concentration drops fivefold, conductivity drops roughly fivefold while molar conductivity increases slightly. Thus, \(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\) and \(\Lambda_{m} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q54 - Dissociation constant of 0.001028 M acetic acid

questiontext.text: The conductivity of \(0.001028\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) acetic acid is \(4.95 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\). If \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) for acetic acid is \(390.5\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), calculate its dissociation constant \(K_{a}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(c = 0.001028\text{ mol L}^{-1}\), \(\kappa = 4.95 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\), \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ} = 390.5\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Acetic acid is a weak monobasic acid with \(\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}, \quad \alpha = \frac{\Lambda_{m}}{\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}}, \quad K_{a} = \frac{c\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Lambda_{m} = \frac{4.95 \times 10^{-5} \times 1000}{0.001028} = 48.15\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\]
\[\alpha = \frac{48.15}{390.5} = 0.1233\]
\[K_{a} = \frac{0.001028 \times (0.1233)^{2}}{1 - 0.1233} = \frac{1.563 \times 10^{-5}}{0.8767} = 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The value \(1.78 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) matches the standard \(K_{a}\) of acetic acid at \(298\text{ K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q55 - Dissociation constant of 0.00241 M acetic acid

questiontext.text: The conductivity of \(0.00241\text{ M}\) acetic acid is \(7.896 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\). If \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) for acetic acid is \(390.5\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), what are its molar conductivity and dissociation constant \(K_{a}\)?

Both \(\Lambda_{m} = 32.76\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and \(K_{a} = 1.85 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) are consistent with weak acid dissociation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q56 - Number of electrons flowing in a metallic wire

questiontext.text: If a steady current of \(0.5\text{ A}\) flows through a metallic wire for \(2\text{ hours}\), how many electrons flow through the wire (take \(e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\))?

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Steady direct current flows for the entire duration.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[Q = I \times t, \quad N = \frac{Q}{e}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[Q = 0.5\text{ A} \times 7200\text{ s} = 3600\text{ C}\]
\[N = \frac{3600\text{ C}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}} = 2.247 \times 10^{22}\text{ electrons}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(3600\text{ C} \approx 0.0373\text{ F}\), and \(0.0373 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 2.247 \times 10^{22}\). Thus, \(2.247 \times 10^{22}\) electrons flow through the wire.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q58 - Time required to deposit silver in series cells

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q60 - Substances capable of oxidising ferrous ions

questiontext.text: Given \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{I}_{2}/\mathrm{I}^{-}} = +0.54\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Br}_{2}/\mathrm{Br}^{-}} = +1.09\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cl}_{2}/\mathrm{Cl}^{-}} = +1.36\text{ V}\), and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}} = +1.51\text{ V}\), which set of three substances can oxidise \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) under standard conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Any species whose standard reduction potential is higher than \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\) can oxidise \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{Br}_{2}\) (\(+1.09\text{ V}\)), \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\) (\(+1.36\text{ V}\)), and \(\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}\) (\(+1.51\text{ V}\)) all have \(E^{\ominus} > +0.77\text{ V}\), whereas \(\mathrm{I}_{2}\) (\(+0.54\text{ V}\)) has \(E^{\ominus} < +0.77\text{ V}\) and cannot oxidise \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{Br}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}\) can oxidise \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q61 - Maximum standard cell potential among metal couples

questiontext.text: Using the standard reduction potentials: \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\), \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\), and \(E^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}} = -2.36\text{ V}\), which galvanic cell combination produces the highest standard cell potential?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\ominus}_{\text{anode}}\) is maximised by pairing the highest \(E^{\ominus}\) cathode with the lowest \(E^{\ominus}\) anode.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pairing \(\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}\) (\(+0.80\text{ V}\)) as cathode and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}\) (\(-2.36\text{ V}\)) as anode gives \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = 0.80 - (-2.36) = 3.16\text{ V}\), which is larger than any other pair.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\mathrm{Mg(s)} \mid \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \parallel \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\) produces the highest standard cell potential.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q62 - Molar conductivity of 0.050 M NaCl in SI units

questiontext.text: The conductivity of a \(0.050\text{ M}\) aqueous \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) solution at \(298\text{ K}\) is \(55.53 \times 10^{-2}\text{ S m}^{-1}\). What is its molar conductivity in \(\mathrm{S\ m^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molarity \(= 0.050\text{ mol L}^{-1}\), conductivity \(\kappa = 55.53 \times 10^{-2}\text{ S m}^{-1} = 0.5553\text{ S m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Convert concentration from \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\) to \(\text{mol m}^{-3}\) using \(1\text{ m}^{3} = 1000\text{ L}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[c = 1000 \times \text{molarity}, \quad \Lambda_{m} = \frac{\kappa}{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[c = 1000 \times 0.050 = 50\text{ mol m}^{-3}\]
\[\Lambda_{m} = \frac{0.5553\text{ S m}^{-1}}{50\text{ mol m}^{-3}} = 0.011106\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 111.06 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(111.06 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) equals \(111.06\text{ S cm}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), which is physically consistent for \(0.050\text{ M NaCl}\). Thus, \(\Lambda_{m} = 111.06 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^{2}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
